content: Meckel syndrome type 1, also referred to as MKS1, is a protein in humans that is encoded by the MKS1 gene. The MKS1 protein, along with another protein called meckelin, is an integral component of the basal body proteome of the flagellar apparatus. These proteins are essential for the proper formation of cilia. Mutations in the MKS1 gene are associated with the development of Meckel syndrome and Bardet-Biedl syndrome, both of which are severe genetic disorders. To study the function of MKS1, model organisms have been utilized. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Mks1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program is a large-scale mutagenesis initiative designed to produce and distribute animal models of human diseases to researchers worldwide. Both male and female mice from this knockout line underwent a standardized phenotypic screening to assess the effects of the gene deletion. A total of 25 tests were conducted on the mutant mice, and two significant abnormalities were identified. Homozygous mutant embryos, observed during gestation, exhibited polydactyly (extra digits), edema (swelling), and defects in the eyes or craniofacial structures. None of these embryos survived to the weaning stage. The remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant adult mice, and no additional abnormalities were detected in this group.
